metadata.name: tree
metadata.description: Display directory structure as a tree

installation.note: tree is not installed by default on most Linux distributions

overview.summary: tree displays directory structures in a tree-like format, making it easy to visualize the hierarchy of files and directories. It's particularly useful for understanding project structure and finding files in nested directories.
when_to_use: Find files in complex directory trees
Get an overview of a directory

syntax.description: Display directory tree for DIRECTORY (or current directory if omitted). Various options control depth, filtering, and output format.

options.use_case: Show only directory structure without files

options.description: Max depth of directory tree to display
options.use_case: Limit tree depth to 2 levels (useful for large trees)
Exclude node_modules and .git from tree output
Include hidden files and directories in tree output

options.description: Print full path prefix for each file
options.use_case: Show full absolute paths instead of relative paths

options.description: Print sizes in human readable format
options.use_case: Show sizes in KB, MB, GB (combine with -s)
Show only files matching a pattern (e.g., only .txt files)

examples.title: Basic directory tree
examples.description: Display tree structure of current directory
examples.output:
.
├── file1.txt
├── file2.txt
├── dir1
│   ├── file3.txt
│   └── subdir
│       └── file4.txt
└── dir2
    └── file5.txt

elements.meaning: Branch connecting to next item at same level

output_explanation.notes: The tree structure clearly shows parent-child relationships and directory hierarchy

examples.title: Limit depth
examples.output:

├── dir1
│   ├── file3.txt
│   └── subdir

misconceptions.title: tree shows file contents
misconceptions.misconception: tree displays file contents like cat
misconceptions.reality: tree only shows directory structure and file/directory names, not file contents. Use cat, less, or editors to view file contents.
misconceptions.tip: tree = structure only. Use cat/less/head/tail to view file contents.

misconceptions.title: tree is installed by default
misconceptions.misconception: tree is available on all Linux systems
misconceptions.reality: tree is not installed by default on most distributions. Install it with: sudo apt install tree (or equivalent for your distro).
misconceptions.tip: Install tree first: sudo apt install tree, then use it.

common_pitfalls.description: tree can be slow on huge directory trees
common_pitfalls.solution: Use -L to limit depth, or -I to ignore large subdirectories. Or use find with -type d for similar effect.

common_pitfalls.description: Large projects produce overwhelming tree output
common_pitfalls.solution: Use -L to limit depth (e.g., -L 2), or -I to exclude patterns. Or pipe to less: tree | less

common_pitfalls.description: tree shows node_modules, build/, dist/ making output cluttered
common_pitfalls.solution: Use -I flag: tree -I 'node_modules|build|dist|.git' to exclude common build/artifact directories

related_commands.relationship: Find files; tree shows structure, find searches
related_commands.description: Find files by name or criteria (complements tree's visual structure)

related_commands.relationship: List files; tree shows hierarchy, ls shows flat list
related_commands.description: List directory contents (tree shows structured hierarchy)

related_commands.relationship: Disk usage; tree shows structure, du shows sizes
related_commands.description: Show disk usage (tree -s combines structure with sizes)

best_practices: Use -L to limit depth for large projects
Use -I to exclude common directories (node_modules, .git, build, etc.)
Use -d to show only directory structure without files
Use -sh to see file sizes in human-readable format
Pipe to less for long output: tree | less
Save tree output: tree > structure.txt to document project layout
Use -a to include hidden files when needed
performance_tips: tree is fast for small to medium directory trees
Use -L to limit depth - significantly faster for large trees
Use -I to skip large subdirectories (like node_modules)
For very large directories, consider find instead

additional_notes.installation: tree is not installed by default - install with: sudo apt install tree
additional_notes.output_format: Uses Unicode box-drawing characters for tree structure (│ ├ └)
additional_notes.pattern_matching: -I and -P support regex patterns for filtering
additional_notes.alternatives: If tree not available, use: find . -print | sed 's;[^/]*/;|____;g;s;____|; |;g'
additional_notes.documentation: Common use: tree -I 'node_modules|.git' > project-structure.txt to document project layout
